Chapter 6: Embedding Simplicity—Making the Practices a Daily Habit
Now that you know the core practices, the real challenge is making them part of your everyday routine. It’s one thing to set clear goals or give someone a compliment once in a while—but turning these actions into habits? That’s a whole different ballgame.
The secret is to treat these practices just like brushing your teeth or checking your calendar—something you do without even thinking about it.
It all starts with intention. As a leader, you need to make a conscious choice to look for chances to clarify, recognize, and correct. With time, these actions blend into the natural rhythm of your day.
Picture this: a manager kicks off each morning by glancing over team goals. Throughout the day, they take a few minutes to walk around, spot great work, and offer quick feedback. And when a problem pops up? They don’t wait for the next meeting—they handle it right then and there.
If you want these habits to really stick, try a few gentle reminders:
Keep goal statements in plain sight—maybe on your desk, in a shared doc, or up on a team board.
Make it a habit to spend just a couple of minutes each day looking for something to praise.
And use a simple checklist to note when you’ve given feedback—whether it’s positive or corrective.
Think of these reminders as helpful guideposts, not strict rules. What you’re aiming for is a culture where clarity, recognition, and accountability happen as naturally as saying hello in the morning. Little by little, these simple actions start to shape how people think and work together.
Here’s a quick example: In a busy retail store, the manager posts daily sales targets right in the break room. She makes a point to thank team members who go the extra mile for customers. If someone forgets to restock a shelf, she addresses it right away, explains the impact, and encourages improvement. These quick, consistent moments keep everyone focused and motivated—even when things get hectic.
By weaving these practices into daily routines, leaders set the stage for lasting benefits—higher morale, better performance, and stronger relationships. And because the approach is so simple, it’s easy to stick with, no matter how much your team grows or things change.
